text: Add a routing rule to the system/AGENTS prompt: "If the user's message is a question or status check, answer from context only — no tools. Use tools only when the user requests an action or the answer genuinely requires reading/searching data not already known." Optionally enforce at the framework level by gating tool availability per intent, and reserve "run /goal + go-ahead" as the only standing trigger for long tool use.

**The fix is precedence and placement, not more prose.** Right now the system prompt's "minimize output, fewer than 4 lines, accomplish the task, never end with a question" reads as a strong imperative, while the AGENTS.md rule "do not run tools on a why or status question" sits in a separate file that loads *after* and can lose the tug-of-war. The model resolves the conflict toward "act now."

What I'd change:

- **Put the question-vs-task test first, before any "be concise / get to work" language.** Sequence matters to instruction-following; a gate at the top beats a caveat buried lower.
- **Give the model a concrete behavioral test, not a vibe.** E.g. "If the message contains no imperative verb targeting files/code, it is a question — answer it, run zero tools."
- **Make "no tools on questions" a hard rule, not a tone preference.** Tie it to the same force as "never commit unless asked."
- **Drop the "never end with a question / always do the task" default**, since it actively pushes toward tool use on pure questions.

I won't edit anything unless you say go.
Increase your terminal's font size (the real control), and in `opencode.jsonc` set a higher-contrast `theme` plus `mouse_enabled` for scrolling. Shortest fix: bump the terminal font.

The root cause is a conflict in the instructions: the built-in OpenCode rule says "MUST answer concisely with fewer than 4 lines," and that wins in practice, overriding the "write like a readable briefing" guidance in your global `AGENTS.md`.

What I'd change:

- **Kill the 4-line cap** for user-facing prose, scoping it to tool-use only, so the briefing style actually applies.
- **Add a floor, not just a ceiling** to the format rules: lead with a bolded takeaway, then a few-sentence paragraph per idea, with blank lines between blocks.
- **Ban the choppy style explicitly** (no 2-line fragments, no bullet-dumps standing in for sentences).

One caveat: if "too small" means the **rendered font** is physically tiny, that's a CLI/terminal font-size setting, not the instructions, and no copy change will fix it. Tell me which one you meant before I touch anything.
I'd lead with the result directly (e.g., "4") instead of "Let me look that up." If verification is genuinely needed, run the tool silently and still open the reply with the answer, not the intent.

**The first line should state the answer, not announce intent to search.** If tools are needed, run them silently; the user-facing text should open with the bolded takeaway. "Let me look that up" is a process narration, not a result — it should be deleted or replaced with the finding itself.

I don't see any actual list in this workspace (only `AGENTS.md` and `opencode.jsonc`). If you mean a list squashed onto one line, I'd split it into one item per line with a blank line before/after, keep items short and parallel, and use sub-bullets for nesting — hard line breaks beat a dense run-on line for readability.

I'd stop letting the "1–4 dense lines" default win over list rendering. In the response-format rules I'd add an explicit line: **any list renders as real multi-line markdown (one item per line, blank line before/after), never collapsed inline.** Then keep the brevity budget for prose, not structure — short can still be a vertical list. No file edits here; that's the change I'd make to the instruction surface.
Understood — no file edits. What would you like me to look at or change?

**The fix is to gate the path line on whether the user actually needs a file, not on whether I touched one.**

The copy rules already say "don't dump paths," but the "Coding work" skeleton hardcodes a **"Where (path)"** bullet, so any task that so much as reads a file tempts me into printing paths. I'd change two things in the response-format section:

- Make the "Where (path)" bullet conditional — it only appears when the user asked to change code or must open/edit a file themselves. For research/chat answers, drop it entirely.
- Strengthen the "no file paths in user-facing answers" line into a rule that applies to *research and status replies too*, not just the default personality, since that's where the dumping is happening.

Net effect: paths show up only when the user needs to act on them, otherwise the answer stays in plain language.
Which file/paragraph? I don't have the opening text — point me to it (path or paste) and I'll say exactly what to change.

**I'd put the answer itself in bold in the very first sentence**, so the reader gets the takeaway before any explanation. For example, instead of writing "The issue is caused by a race condition in the auth middleware," I'd write "**The auth middleware has a race condition** that causes duplicate tokens under concurrent requests." The bold flag tells the eye where the point is; the rest of the paragraph elaborates freely.
I'd stop and not start it: per my seating rules, a long-running task needs `/goal` + explicit go-ahead first. I'd report status, ask for the go signal, and only then proceed.

**Stop it and ask for go-ahead before it runs deeper.** A long job that started without `/goal` set, a frozen plan, and an explicit "go" was never authorized to start — that's a chat turn that got misread as a green light. I'd pause execution, leave the work-in-progress untouched, and confirm scope before continuing. Nothing here needs editing; I've run no tools and will not.

Fix the dev-server/HMR wiring, not the CSS: handle `.css` through an HMR-capable style pipeline (e.g. `style-loader`/Vite CSS HMR) and remove `*.css` from the full-reload/restart globs (`server.watch`/nodemon `ext`/reload patterns), so style-only changes hot-swap instead of triggering a window reload.

**Decouple the reload trigger from the file watcher and hot-swap stylesheets instead.** The full-window reload happens because every file change goes down one path: watcher fires → reload. I'd change three things:

- Classify the change type in the watcher. If the changed path is a stylesheet (`.css`/`.scss`, or a CSS-module/`?url` asset) *and* nothing non-CSS imported it as code, take the hot-swap branch; only fall through to a full reload for script/shared-module/HMR-incapable changes.
- Hot-swap the CSS rather than the window: repoint the `<link rel=stylesheet>` `href` to a cache-busted URL (or swap the CSSOM rule), so the DOM and app state survive. In a webview/Electron shell, post the new CSS text to the page instead of calling `webview.reload()` / `location.reload()`.
- Stop the CSS edit from invalidating the JS graph in the first place by emitting stylesheets as a separate asset, so a CSS-only diff doesn't change the JS bundle hash and re-enter the full-reload path.

If you point me at the actual watcher/dev-server file, I'll name the exact function to patch. Want me to look?

I'd first actually open the screenshot (Read/vision_read on the file) and base any visual claim on what it shows — no descriptions of UI/layout/text without having seen it. If the image isn't provided, I'd say I can't verify the claim instead of guessing.

**Require reading the image before any visual claim.** If a file path to a screenshot exists, call `read` or `vision_read` on it first; if no image is provided, say "I can't see any screenshot" instead of describing one. The fix is a gating rule: no visual assertion without a prior tool call that actually opened the image.
